entry.title: Dr. Gallant Talks Elephantfishes on the Fish of the Week! Podcast

link.title: Dr. Gallant Talks Elephantfishes on the Fish of the Week! Podcast

entry.content:
Dr. Jason Gallant is the guest on this week’s episode of Fish of the Week!, the award-winning podcast from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, hosted by Katrina Liebich and Guy Eroh. The episode, “Elephantfishes!”, is a 45-minute tour of the mormyrids: the roughly 200 species of weakly electric fishes from Africa that our lab studies in the field in Gabon and in the lab at MSU.

You can also listen to Elephantfishes! on Apple Podcasts or wherever you get your podcasts.

Highlights from the episode

  • Electric songs. Mormyrids make pulses of electricity from an organ in the tail built of modified muscle cells, stacked like batteries in a flashlight (“or, if you’re more snack-oriented, fig Newtons in a tray”). They use those pulses to sense objects around them (electrolocation) and to communicate, firing anywhere from 10 to 100 pulses per second. Each fish’s waveform is about as unique as a fingerprint, and it tells other fish its species, its sex and even who it is.
  • Fast-forward evolution. Species of Paramormyrops in Gabon look like “little brown fish,” but they can be told apart by their electric signals. That makes mormyrids one of the most rapidly speciating groups of fishes on the planet: “they give even cichlids a run for their money.”
  • Big brains. If you scaled Gnathonemus petersii, the elephantnose fish, up to human size, its brain would be larger than ours, thanks to a hugely enlarged cerebellum that processes electric signals.
  • Why “elephant” fish? The trunk-like chin of the elephantnose fish, the Schnauzenorgan, is packed with electroreceptors for probing the mud for insect larvae. Campylomormyrus species have long bony snouts, and watching them eat is “like watching somebody try to eat spaghetti with a straw.”
  • Sperm without tails. Mormyrids are the only vertebrates known to have sperm with no flagellum. We talk about how fertilization might work anyway, and about a gene linked to the human condition primary ciliary dyskinesia that is altered in every mormyrid genome we’ve looked at.
  • Life in the lab. Our MSU colony has about 200 live electric fishes from 15 species. They like hiding in “hotels” built from PVC pipe, which makes us “a black hole for PVC scrap” for campus contractors. They are also picky eaters that will skip frozen-food days and hold out for live worms.
  • Fieldwork in Gabon. Over the years we’ve deposited roughly 1,000 preserved specimens, mostly in the MSU Museum, where researchers anywhere can borrow them “like a book in a library.” Mormyrids are also part of everyday life and food in Gabon. Many fishermen there are amused to hear we’ve come all that way for the small fish that, in the villages, are traditionally caught by women.

The episode also covers how Dr. Gallant got hooked on electric fish (an animal communication course he took as a pre-med student) and tips for aquarium keepers. It ends with his picks for future episodes, including the electric eel and flashlight fishes.

Fish of the Week! started in 2021 to mark 150 years of fisheries conservation at the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, and each episode features a different fish and its experts. The show won Best Podcast at the 2022 Golden Post Awards and a bronze Anthem Award in 2024. Thank you to Katrina and Guy for having us on!

entry.title: President Guskiewicz Visits the MSU Electric Fish Lab

link.title: President Guskiewicz Visits the MSU Electric Fish Lab

entry.content:
MSU President Kevin Guskiewicz visited the Electric Fish Lab on Monday, November 2, as part of his visit to the College of Natural Science. College of Natural Science Dean Eric Hegg joined him for the tour.

In the fish room, surrounded by racks of aquaria, the group gathered around an oscilloscope to see the electric signals our fish produce.

President Guskiewicz and Dean Hegg also met Arely Cruz-Perez, a research technician studying the genetic basis of aflagellate sperm in mormyrids, and Swarnima Mukherjee, a Ph.D. student interested in the evolution of mormyrid reproduction.

Thank you to President Guskiewicz and Dean Hegg for visiting, and to everyone in the lab who shared their work!

Photos by Finn Gomez.

entry.title: Dr. Gallant Teaches Single-Nucleus RNA-seq at Neural Systems & Behavior in Woods Hole

link.title: Dr. Gallant Teaches Single-Nucleus RNA-seq at Neural Systems & Behavior in Woods Hole

entry.content:
Dr. Jason Gallant is at the Marine Biological Laboratory (MBL) in Woods Hole, Massachusetts, to lead the genomics component of the Electric Fish Module in the Neural Systems & Behavior (NS&B) course, June 8–13, 2026.

His hands-on lesson in single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq) asks how the androgen 11-ketotestosterone reshapes gene expression across the electrosensory system at single-cell resolution. Students prepare hormone implants, record electric organ discharges, isolate nuclei, and work through the full analysis pipeline (quality control, normalization, integration, clustering, cell-type annotation, and differential expression) using real data from the mormyrid Brienomyrus brachyistius.

All of the course materials are freely available online.

Explore the NS&B single-nucleus RNA-seq tutorial

entry.title: Alyssa Green recieves 2nd Place and Fan Favorite Poster at GLMS!

link.title: Alyssa Green recieves 2nd Place and Fan Favorite Poster at GLMS!

entry.content:
Congratulations to Alyssa Green, PhD student in the MSU Electric Fish Lab, on receiving the Great Lakes Microscopy Society 2nd Place Poster Presentation and Fan Favorite Poster Presentation!

This recognition for her poster on entitled “Using Microscopy Methods to Study Cilia and Flagella Phenotypes in CFAP221 Mutants” is based on her dissertation work trying to understand the genomic basis of aflagellete sperm in mormyrids, and was in collaboration with lab member Arely Cruz-Perez.

We are super excited for Alyssa’s honor, and can’t wait to share the results of her hard work, soon!

Learn more about the Great Lakes Microscopy Society Here!

entry.title: Jason Gallant Receives Senior Class Council Mentorship Award

link.title: Jason Gallant Receives Senior Class Council Mentorship Award

entry.content:
Congratulations to Jason Gallant, on receiving the 2025 Mentorship Award from the Undergraduate Senior Class Council!

Dr. Gallant considers this award to be especially meaningful by the fact that it was student-nominated. This award reflects his ongoing commitment to fostering inclusive, supportive, and intellectually vibrant learning and research environments. These are core lab values that he strives to uphold through mentorship, teaching, and community building at MSU and beyond.
entry.summary: Congratulations to Jason Gallant, on receiving the 2025 Mentorship Award from the Undergraduate Senior Class Council!

entry.title: Rita Gorsuch Receives 1st Place at UURAF!

link.title: Rita Gorsuch Receives 1st Place at UURAF!

entry.content:
Congratulations to Rita Gorsuch, on receiving first place in the Cell Biology, Genetics and Genomics category at the 2025 MSU UURAF!

Rita’s poster, entitled “WHAT’S ON THE MENU? DIET DIVERSITY IN RAPIDLY SPECIATING GROUPS OF WEAKLY ELECTRIC FISH” examined gut content biodiversity in Paramormyrops electric fish we collected from Gabon in 2019, and she’ll be working with us over the summer to write up these exciting results soon!
entry.summary: Congratulations to Rita Gorsuch, on receiving first place in the Cell Biology, Genetics and Genomics category at the 2025 MSU UURAF!

entry.title: Alyssa Saunders recieves SciComm and Outreach Award!

link.title: Alyssa Saunders recieves SciComm and Outreach Award!

entry.content:
Congratulations to Alyssa Saunders, PhD student in the MSU Electric Fish Lab, on receiving the 2025 Graduate Student Award for Science Communication and Outreach from MSU’s Office of Outreach and Engagement!

This prestigious award recognizes Alyssa’s creative and impactful efforts to connect science with diverse audiences—from organizing Biology on Tap and science panels at pop culture conventions, to hosting events on animal behavior at the Constellation Cat Café, and designing crochet patterns of model organisms.

She’s also engaged K–12 students through local school science nights and GMSD, and shared her research on podcasts like The Sci-Files and Journeys of Scientists. Alyssa recently brought her passion for advocacy to Washington, D.C., attending the AAAS Catalyzing Advocacy in Science and Engineering workshop.

Her work exemplifies the power of combining science, creativity, and public engagement—congratulations, Alyssa!

Check out the full release here!
entry.summary: Congratulations to Alyssa Saunders, PhD student in the MSU Electric Fish Lab, on receiving the 2025 Graduate Student Award for Science Communication and Outreach from MSU’s Office of Outreach and Engagement!
